paper_title: Behind Video Generation: Observations and Insights on Multimodal Understanding from Kling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video generation has progressed from isolated clips to coherent short-form audiovisual sequences, and the bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. This report summarizes the observations and insights on multimodal understanding gained from successive generations of Kling. We argue that generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data--conditioning--alignment--evaluation chain, and we examine this chain module by module. Kling-MLLM, a shared multimodal foundation model that unifies image, video, audio, synchronized audio--video, and interleaved inputs, is specialized for each downstream module. Because a DiT is trained on far fewer training samples than a language model, we treat captioning as a semantic contract that maximizes description density, and extend it to reference-grounded captioning that makes reference bindings explicit. Prompt enhancement translates user intent into this caption distribution: basic PE is derived from captions of compelling videos and refined with text-level and generator-in-the-loop reinforcement learning, while agentic PE refines the story and retrieves compelling examples. We show that a reliable text encoder comes from perceptual training rather than from stronger language ability, and that candidates can be screened from text alone before end-to-end training. Reward modeling pairs a general reward model for explainable, localized critiques with a decision reward model for fast multidimensional scoring, treating perceptual bandwidth as a first-class design parameter. Finally, we review task-specific automatic evaluation, focusing on protocols that expose scoring shortcuts and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack behind controllable video generation.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Over four years, video generation has passed through several distinct regimes. In 2023, general-purpose video creation remained largely aspirational. In 2024, early systems produced compelling demonstrations, but with limited reliability and control. By 2025, leading models could generate production-usable shots and creative assets. By 2026, frontier systems had begun to produce usable short-form audiovisual sequences that coordinate multiple shots, persistent subjects, performance, camera language, dialogue, music, and sound. The unit by which progress is judged has expanded from the frame to the clip, then to the shot, and now to the complete sequence. This expansion changes the technical problem. Quality at the frame or clip level can often be assessed locally, whereas usefulness at the sequence level is compositional: constraints interact, errors accumulate over time, and decisions in one shot affect the interpretation of the next. The system must infer latent creative specification from heterogeneous inputs, express it as conditions the generator can execute, and evaluate the result at the same semantic granularity. Multimodal understanding has evolved accordingly, from coarse textvideo correspondence to dense spatiotemporal description, reference grounding, creative planning, and multidimensional judgment, and it has helped make synthesis controllable and usable. General-purpose multimodal benchmarks capture only part of this requirement. High aggregate scores in visual question answering (VQA) do not imply reliable understanding of camera language, leftright relations, composition, lighting, shot boundaries, identity binding, or dense temporal change. These capabilities are weakly represented in standard supervision, yet they determine whether generated result is controllable and editable; evaluation research has shifted in the same direction, from superficial realism toward controllability, commonsense, and physical faithfulness [1, 69]. For video generation, the question is therefore not whether multimodal large language model (MLLM) is broadly capable, but which semantics reach the generator, through what representation, and with what evidence of downstream benefit. This perspective is grounded in our work on Kling 1.0 through Kling 4.0 [50], together with Kling AI Avatar [51] and Kling Motion Control [52]. Across these releases, we specialized Kling-MLLM, our shared multimodal foundation model, into captioners, prompt enhancement (PE) models, text encoders, reward models, and automatic evaluators, as requirements progressed from basic textvideo correspondence to reference binding, identity preservation, motion transfer, precise editing, audiovisual synchronization, and complete video generation. As generation capabilities advanced, progress depended increasingly on understanding what to generate, what to preserve, how to organize it over time, and how to verify the result. Our central thesis is: Video generation quality is the projection of multimodal understanding through the entire data conditioningalignmentevaluation chain. An observed generation failure is not, by itself, diagnosis. The same symptom may originate from caption that omits the relevant supervision, conditioning representation that discards temporal structure, reward model that favors smooth but static motion, or an evaluator that never tests the requested event. We therefore treat multimodal understanding as property of the entire chain rather than as score attached to single model. This perspective leads to four claims: The bottleneck is shifting from rendering to semantic control. Improvements in visual fidelity do not automatically yield correct actions, camera language, reference binding, or narrative continuity. Generation-oriented understanding is an independent axis of progress. Data efficiency depends on description density. diffusion transformer (DiT) is trained on far fewer samples than language model, and both training throughput and the supply of usable video preclude closing this gap through scaling. Each training video must therefore carry as much supervision as possible, which makes the density of textual description per unit of video duration the central measure of data efficiency. Dense, generation-oriented captions and reference-grounded captions with explicit bindings are designed to maximize this density, and perception-tuned text encoder ensures that it actually reaches the generator. mature DiT has sweet spot, and agentic methods help reach it. Trained on dense captions, the generator responds best to conditions written in its caption distribution, and mature model can usually realize the users request from description in this distribution. Basic PE translates requests into this distribution, but single PE model has limited capacity and may fail to capture the vividness of compelling videos, while

Agentic PE, such as story refinement that repairs contradictory requests and retrieval of captions of compelling videos, divides this work and improves reasonableness, faithfulness, and vividness together. Evaluation should follow the task. Because failure can originate anywhere in the chain, single aggregate score says little about its source. Generation tasks differ in their success criteria and in the shortcuts that inflate scores, so evaluation protocols should be task-specific and decomposed into directly observable criteria. Inexpensive proxies, such as text-only encoder screening and text-level PE verifiers, can filter candidates before costly end-to-end training. Together, these practices make failures easier to trace upstream. The following sections trace this chain from Kling-MLLM through standard and reference-grounded captioning, PE, text encoding, and reward modeling, and conclude with review of task-specific evaluation practices. Each module section follows the same discipline: observation, mechanism, and engineering implication. Our aim is to explain how advances in multimodal understanding became deployable capabilities across successive generations of Kling, and which aspects of that experience may generalize beyond single model family.

sections.title: 2.1 Objective and Scope
sections.content: The multimodal understanding foundation model serves as the shared perception and reasoning backbone for Klings image-generation, video-generation, image-editing, and video-editing tasks. It is not tied to single endpoint. Instead, the foundation checkpoints are specialized through task-specific post-training for use as captioners, PE models, reward models, text encoders, and other experts. This design centralizes visual, temporal, and acoustic knowledge in reusable base model while allowing each upstream task to select an appropriate accuracylatency operating point. We refer to this model as Kling-MLLM; it unifies images, videos, audio, synchronized audiovideo, and arbitrarily interleaved media in one autoregressive interface.

sections.title: 2.2 Kling-MLLM Architecture
sections.content: The Kling-MLLM family comprises dense 27B variant and two mixture-of-experts (MoE) variants, 35B-A3B and 397B-A17B. Across scales and development iterations, the large language model (LLM) and vision backbones are initialized from compatible checkpoints in the Qwen3.5Qwen3.8 model families [39]. Starting from these checkpoints, we add scale-dependent audio towers, described in Audio below. We also redesign the modality-processing logic for images, videos, audio, synchronized audiovideo, and interleaved media, and conduct multimodal mid-training to obtain the Kling-MLLM foundation models. At the input interface, every supported stream is mapped to common sequence consumed by single LLM (Figure 2). The visual path consists of ViT, spatial pooling, and vision aligner. The audio path uses scale-dependent audio tower and projects its output to the LLM hidden width. Consequently, the LLM can process text, visual embeddings, and acoustic embeddings in single sequence without quantizing the input media into shared discrete codebook. Text and interleaved records. Text is segmented by the native LLM tokenizer and mapped through its embedding table. Modality-specific boundary tokens make each span self-delimiting, so multiple images, videos, and audio clips can appear at arbitrary positions in one context. Images are processed at dynamic resolution while preserving their aspect ratios. The Images and videos. resolution is selected jointly with the available context budget, allowing the model to retain useful visual detail without requiring fixed input shape. Videos use both dynamically selected frame rate and frame count. The processor adapts these choices to the videos duration and the available context, while sampling across the full temporal range so that short and long videos can be represented efficiently. The selected frames follow the same dynamic-resolution path as images and are encoded into visual-token blocks. Each block is associated with its frames physical timestamp, enabling the LLM to reason about event order and temporal location without fixed sampling assumptions.

Multimodal inputs are encoded by visual and audio paths into aligned continuous tokens, delimited by modality boundary markers, anchored with physical timestamps, and interleaved with text before entering the LLM backbone. The audio path illustrates the dual-branch MelVAE tower used in larger variants. Sync A-V denotes synchronized audiovideo input. Audio. Kling-MLLM uses two scale-dependent audio towers. For smaller model variants, the tower follows the Qwen3-Omni design [63]: 16-kHz monaural waveform is converted to Mel spectrogram and encoded as 13 audio tokens per second. Larger model variants instead use dual-branch tower that fuses Mel and waveform-VAE features. For each clip, the data pipeline supplies two time-aligned views: 16-kHz, 128-bin Mel spectrogram at 100 frames per second and 44.1-kHz waveform for an in-house VAE. Conv1d front end maps the Mel stream to the target 25-token-per-second grid. In parallel, the VAE latent sequence is linearly interpolated along the temporal axis to match the Mel-branch token grid, then normalized and projected to the Mel hidden width. learned scalar gate adds these aligned VAE features residually to the Mel features. Positional encoding and the audio Transformer operate on the fused sequence, after which the output projection maps it to LLM-width embeddings ZA RLAd at 25 audio tokens per second. The two tower designs therefore expose the same embedding interface to the LLM. The processor instantiates audio-boundary, timestamp-injection, and synchronized audiovideo serialization at the selected towers token rate. Audio boundary markers delimit each span, and absolute timestamps provide temporal anchors for long audio sequences. Audio timestamp injection. Within each audio branch, the acoustic-token rate is fixed, so elapsed time is in principle recoverable from token position. In practice, however, this implicit clock provides insufficient temporal control: the language model does not always convert token indices into reliable absolute-time estimates, which weakens duration awareness and temporal grounding. Prompting experiments with Gemini APIs [11] support this interpretation: explicitly providing the total audio duration in the prompt produces marked improvement in temporal grounding. The adopted representation places explicit start and end timestamps around each audio span and inserts absolute-time anchors every five seconds. The boundary timestamps expose the clip duration directly, while the periodic anchors reduce the interval over which time must be inferred and support fine-grained event localization. They also align the temporal organization of audio with synchronized audiovideo sequences, where acoustic and visual tokens share timestamped timeline.

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: Synchronized audiovideo. Audio and video are serialized jointly inside one synchronized multimedia element, rather than represented as two separate media elements. Each processed video frame forms an atomic visual-token block whose tokens share the frame timestamp, while individual audio tokens retain timestamps determined by the audio-token rate. The processor traverses the video frames chronologically and, before each visual block, inserts all audio tokens that occur after the preceding frame and no later than the current frame. Thus, the original order within each modality is preserved, and an audio token is placed before visual block when they have the same timestamp. sections.title: 2.3 Four-Stage Training Curriculum
sections.content: Training follows curriculum that broadens multimodal supervision and progressively increases temporal coverage and context capacity. Stage 1: acoustic initialization. The vision tower and LLM are frozen, and only the audio tower is optimized. Its core Training uses short sequence length, and the data mixture consists entirely of audio data. speech component combines Mandarin, English, and multilingual transcription data with spoken question answering, speech-conditioned text continuation, and instruction following. Non-speech audio coverage includes environmental and acoustic events, music, non-verbal vocalizations, speaker and accent attributes, and detailed captioning. Data from concatenated speech, multi-speaker dialogues, emotion-rich conversations, audiobooks, and other long recordings provide longer acoustic contexts. Thus, this stage establishes broad acoustic representation rather than an ASR-only encoder, without perturbing the other pretrained components. Stage 2: joint multimodal training. All three modules are unfrozen, and training uses short sequence length. Audio and synchronized audiovideo data constitute the largest part of the mixture. This is the first stage in which the audio tower and LLM are optimized jointly, so the curriculum deliberately emphasizes audio and synchronized audiovideo data to establish robust acousticlanguage alignment and teach the LLM to integrate temporally synchronized auditory and visual evidence. Audio supervision covers multilingual ASR, spoken question answering and instruction following, environmental sounds, music, timbre, non-verbal vocalizations, and detailed captioning. Synchronized audiovideo examples add joint captioning, transcription, and basic temporal-event alignment. Image, video, text, and other mixed-modality data remain in the mixture at smaller proportions. Their role is to preserve the models visual perception, language understanding, reasoning, and general multimodal capabilities while the acoustic pathway is being integrated, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting. These retained data include dense image and video captioning, edit-instruction inference, multi-image composition, counting, OCR, document and chart understanding, spatial reasoning, and educational and scientific text. Stage 3: temporal-capacity expansion. All modules remain trainable, and training transitions to long sequence length. The mixture shifts toward audio, video, and audiovideo data. Its objective is to improve fine-grained temporal perception. The video sources span movie and general video question answering, timestamped procedural steps, instruction-guided temporal grounding, multi-shot narrative understanding, spatial reasoning, unusual or anomalous action recognition, and playback-speed-sensitive motion. Audio training continues to include multilingual ASR, spoken instructions, sound and music captioning, and audio question answering; synchronized examples add timestamped audiovisual event alignment. Counting, OCR, document and chart understanding remain in the mixture alongside multilingual instruction, mathematical, and multi-domain reasoning data. Additional supervision covers detailed media captioning, shot-boundary understanding, visual artifact localization, and reference-conditioned generation-prompt rewriting. Stage 4: long-context consolidation. Both modality towers are frozen and only the LLM is updated. This stage also uses long sequence length, allowing the model to focus on long-form integration while retaining the frozen modality encoders. The highest-quality data available for every supported modality are placed in this stage, allowing the final LLM update to consolidate capabilities using the cleanest and most reliable supervision. Long-video data provide supervision for retrieval, question answering, multi-span temporal grounding, reference-conditioned search, fine-grained motion, and evidence aggregation over extended timelines. Long-form audio receives parallel treatment through event localization, interval-conditioned description,

sections.content: timestamped summarization, temporal-event reasoning, spoken QA, and soundscape segmentation. Joint audiovisual data emphasize synchronized description, detail recovery, cross-stream reasoning, and constraintfollowing, while interleaved audioimage examples require evidence to be composed across modalities. Visual logic, science, counting, text recognition, document/chart understanding, and general text reasoning remain in the mixture. The capstone stage is designed to help the LLM organize fixed perceptual features over longer evidence chains and return grounded, structured responses. The supervision mix is likewise adjusted by stage. Captioning is combined with recognition, retrieval, localization, structured extraction, question answering, and both direct-response and reasoning-oriented examples. Several large sources are partitioned across successive stages, preserving selected speech, OCR/document, chart, video, and reasoning coverage as new task families are introduced. The curriculum is therefore progression in both modality coupling and task diversity, with increasing temporal and contextual demands, rather than sequence of four disjoint corpora. We also explore model merging and find that merging the Stage 1 and Stage 4 checkpoints yields better checkpoint than either alone.

sections.title: 2.4 Data Construction
sections.content: The training corpus combines public data, Kling-specific task data, and agent-oriented data. At the systemdesign level, heterogeneous sources are represented through common conversation-oriented schema, with media metadata and modality boundaries retained so that one loader can construct image, video, audio, synchronized audiovideo, and interleaved examples, following common practice in omni-modal systems [63]. Public Data Ingestion Public corpora enter three-part workflow: AutoResearch Auto Data Process Auto Revise, with revised records looping back from Auto Revise to Auto Data Process for revalidation. In AutoResearch, one search agent monitors Hugging Face Daily Papers, filters work on text, image, video, audio, audiovideo, and multimodal foundation models, and extracts candidate datasets from the selected papers. second agent monitors trending Hugging Face datasets. Their results are merged and deduplicated both against one another and against the historical registry. During dataset selection, we also exclude datasets containing sensitive material, datasets whose licenses are incompatible with the intended use, and datasets that overlap with any evaluation set. Papers associated with the remaining candidates are routed for review, while the selected new datasets enter automated processing. Auto Data Process downloads each selected dataset and invokes modality-specific conversion skill for text, image, video, audio, audiovideo, or interleaved-media records. sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: Kling-Specific Task Data Internal task data target the perception and reasoning capabilities required by Klings image and video generation and editing systems. They cover world knowledge through interleaved imagetext records and controlled taxonomy of actions, sounds, subjects, and scenes; image perception through bilingual OCR across diverse text appearances and layouts, counting, grounding, metadata-aware description, and pose understanding; dense image and video captioning of scenes, subjects, motion, style, camera behavior, and multi-shot structure; and editing and reference understanding through paired source target images or videos, instructions for addition, deletion, and modification, and multi-reference conditioning. Multimodal Agent Data The agent-data mixture spans both general-purpose tool use and multimodal perception-to-action tasks. General-agent examples cover multi-step API and transactional workflows, search and evidence-grounded web research, software-engineering and terminal interaction, structured reasoning and data transformation, and safety-aware everyday assistance. Their supervision ranges from complete tool-use loops to partial trajectories for next-action selection and direct responses, training the model to plan dependent actions, interpret tool returns, verify intermediate results, and decide when tool use is necessary. Multimodal-agent examples include image-grounded retrieval and visual reasoning, GUI interaction grounded in screen observations, agentic video understanding that searches and reasons over temporally distributed evidence, and Blender-based tasks involving controllable 3D scenes, objects, motion, camera viewpoints, and rendering. These data may be constructed or augmented with model-generated instructions, trajectories, and responses followed by consistency checks.

sections.title: 3 Caption: From Pixels to Trainable Semantics
sections.content: When training video generator, caption is more than human-readable summary: it is the semantic interface that converts visual evidence into conditional supervision. Omitted details leave controllable factors underspecified, forcing the generator to fall back on dataset priors, whereas inaccurate statements inject conflicting training signals. Building production-grade captioning system therefore requires rethinking both what information captions preserve and how they organize visual and acoustic evidence over time. fluent sentence may correctly identify scene while reversing spatial directions, collapsing sequential actions into single state, hallucinating sounds, or losing subject identity across shots. Figure 3 shows how linguistic fluency conceals supervision errors: the caption recognizes the setting, yet mislabels hard cut as fade, omits the titles timing, misses pre-appearance dialogue, and leaves visible text untranscribed. Such captions may score well on lexical-overlap metrics despite errors that compromise their value as supervision for generation.

sections.title: Observation
sections.content: Traditional captioning leaderboards and production captioning emphasize different objectives. Standard metrics reward linguistic similarity to acceptable references, while training generative models requires faithful, complete, temporally organized, and consistently formatted representations of the source video. This gap is increasingly recognized in the research literature. Standard sentence-level metrics fail to capture hallucinations even in short image captions [41]. As captions become denser, evaluation has shifted from direct sentence matching toward decomposed multidimensional question-answer verification [5]. These efforts suggest that once captions become supervision for generation, evaluation should move from sentence-level resemblance toward verifiable semantic facts. However, evaluation using verifiable questions risks conflating captioning capability with VQA capability. VQA tests whether model can verify specified detail on demand, bypassing the harder problem of deciding what to state on its own. As CAPability shows, models exhibit know but cannot tell gap: strong visual recognition does not guarantee comprehensive autonomous description [34]. Consequently, strong VQA performance alone is insufficient to establish that model can produce effective captions for training. This section formalizes captioning as tightly coupled engineering system comprising four core components: (1) semantic contract specifying what to describe and how to express it; (2) multi-expert production pipeline that distills complex signals into deployable student model; (3) conjunctive acceptance criteria for assessing caption usability; and (4) downstream validation protocols that determine whether improved captions translate into better generation.

Subject identity, action, and temporal order are generally mandatory, while OCR, speech, sound effects, and multi-shot structure should be included only when supported by the input. Furthermore, caption granularity also depends on the downstream use case. Short captions suit retrieval, whereas dense captions provide richer supervision for generation. Mixing the two without clear policy creates an unmanageable training distribution. Even when generating fluent descriptions, models frequently fail on critical dimensions, including spatial relations, camera movement, composition, lighting, and shot boundaries. While often attributed to limited capacity, these failures stem primarily from supervision gaps. Generic datasets prioritize vague aesthetic descriptors such as cinematic lighting and beautiful composition over explicit spatial and technical labels, limiting the benefits of scaling. Long videos further expose temporal failures, including reordered events, merged shots, and inconsistent references. Therefore, video caption should not be viewed as an extended

sections.content: image description but rather as compact temporal data structure. While content dictates which facts enter the supervision signal, writing conventions determine whether those facts form stable, bindable interface for the text encoder and generator. To reliably transmit these semantic details, four formatting practices yield disproportionate engineering leverage: 1. Name entities explicitly and consistently. Use discriminative noun phrases and retain them across sentences and shots. Avoid ambiguous expressions such as he, it, or the other person when the referent may be unclear to the generator. Stable naming improves both textual coreference and visual identity continuity. 2. Treat shot timestamps as alignment signals. Anchor each shot boundary to its corresponding content using monotonic, validated timestamps. Accurate timestamp-content pairs explicitly teach the model when semantic conditions shift. 3. Transcribe visible text faithfully. Preserve original characters and salient styles instead of paraphrasing. Omitting visible text teaches the model that lettering is an uncontrolled texture, while incorrect transcription introduces contradictory supervision. 4. Integrate audio with visual elements temporally. Describe dialogue, salient sound effects, and music at the points where they occur within the visual narrative. Crucially, audio-related fields should be activated only when an audio track has been inspected.

sections.title: 3.2 The Supervision Pipeline: Separating Complex Discovery from Efficient Deployment
sections.content: Satisfying this semantic contract at production scale is beyond what single prompt to proprietary model can deliver. Constructing reliable supervision requires multi-stage pipeline: 1. Inspection and Routing: Videos are classified by content type, duration, motion dynamics, shot density, and audio availability to determine the necessary expert pathways. 2. Perceptual Evidence Preservation: Preprocessing steps such as downsampling, black-frame removal, audio decoding, and OCR/ASR ensure that critical signals remain intact before reaching expert models. 3. Routed Expert Claims: general visual expert identifies subjects and scene content, while specialized models extract specific dimensions, such as camera motion, spatial relations, lighting, and shot boundaries. 4. Integration and Conflict Resolution: The integration layer resolves conflicting expert claims against source evidence, normalizes terminology, assigns stable entity names, and removes redundancy. 5. Conjunctive Quality Gating: Candidates should strictly satisfy thresholds across accuracy, coverage, and diversity, alongside cross-modal and cross-shot consistency checks. Rejected cases flow into difficultyindexed error pool for diagnosis and targeted remediation.

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: Robust supervision originates from orchestrated pipelines. Explicitly mining previously unobserved dimensions and resolving inter-expert conflicts expand semantic coverage and accuracy far more effectively than simply scaling up general-purpose annotator. Although this multi-expert pipeline produces comprehensive and reliable supervision, deploying it directly incurs prohibitive latency because of its serial execution. To address this limitation, the pipelines output should be distilled into single-pass student model. This reduces the deployment footprint while preserving globally consistent entity naming and the semantic contract synthesized by the offline factory.

sections.title: 3.3 Acceptance Criteria: Conjunctive Quality and Atomic Benchmarking
sections.content: A production-grade caption should satisfy four criteria simultaneously: factual accuracy, semantic coverage, beneficial diversity, and internal consistency. These four criteria are strictly conjunctive: optimizing any single dimension in isolation induces predictable shortcuts and specific generation failures, as illustrated in Table 7.

sections.title: Internal consistency
sections.content: Reuse rigid templates; ignore local nuances Lost dynamic state changes robotic generation To prevent these shortcuts, evaluation should move beyond lexical metrics and test these criteria directly. As CHAIR demonstrates, higher sentence-level scores do not imply fewer hallucinations [41]. This vulnerability is especially pronounced in dense captions, where local errors are easily diluted by surrounding fluent text. Therefore, the appropriate evaluation unit is an atomic, source-grounded information item. Instead of matching surface text, evaluators should verify whether candidate caption correctly expresses predefined essential facts and their temporal scopes. This atomic formulation is largely agnostic to surface phrasing, effectively disentangling the four acceptance criteria that reference-based metrics tend to conflate. comprehensive benchmark should expose at least four complementary views: Content validity: factual precision, semantic coverage, beneficial diversity, and internal consistency; Generation-specific dimensions: action progression, spatial direction, cinematography, composition, lighting, temporal ordering, shot transitions, OCR, speech, and sound; Interface compliance: parse rate, timestamp validity, terminology compliance, and marker validity; Difficulty slices: duration, shot count, entity count, event count, motion speed, OCR density, audio complexity, and content domain. Finally, automatic judges require rigorous stability validation prior to deployment. This entails measuring judgment variance on identical captions, calibrating against human annotations on stratified subsets, and checking ranking robustness across different model families. Crucially, evaluation should control for caption length to prevent judges from conflating verbosity with true semantic coverage. More broadly, the judge model, evaluation prompt, decoding parameters, and preprocessing steps together define the benchmark configuration and should therefore be versioned as part of the evaluation protocol.

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: True superiority withstands granular decomposition. credible improvement specifies which facts are more accurate, which dimensions are more complete, and under which difficulty slices the improvements persist. Gains that vanish when controlling for caption length or appear only in aggregate scores provide insufficient evidence of better supervisory quality.

sections.title: 3.4 Downstream Validation: The Generator as the Final Consumer
sections.content: Intrinsic caption evaluations function as proxies until validated by downstream consumer. Recent benchmarks such as VidCapBench [5] and CapRiCorn-1K [6] demonstrate strong correlations between their evaluation scores and downstream performance, including text-to-video generation quality and video reconstruction fidelity, thereby establishing core experimental principle: caption quality should ultimately be judged by the generative capabilities it enables in the downstream model.

sections.title: Observation
sections.content: Descriptive quality does not automatically translate into supervisory quality. caption may become more readable while exceeding the text encoders effective context, adding details that the generator cannot localize in time, or inflating evaluation scores via generic aesthetic terms. Downstream validation is essential to distinguish superficial linguistic improvement from usable conditional information.

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: Controlled downstream experiments help distinguish usable conditional information from superficial linguistic gains. Matching caption lengths and verified fact counts can reduce confounding effects, while targeted interventions, such as modifying camera-motion descriptions alone, can reveal whether improvements transfer to the corresponding generation capability. Combining human preferences with fine-grained metricsspanning subject identity, action, space, camera, temporal structure, text rendering, audio alignment, and visual qualityexposes specific control failures that global textvideo similarity score obscures. Ultimately, the value of captioning strategy lies in its measurable effect on generation. Small-scale fine-tuning or evaluation with frozen generator provides practical way to assess whether improved captions yield more faithful instruction following before changes are scaled to larger training pipelines.

sections.title: 3.6 Discussion
sections.content: Scaling the captioning system described in this section leaves several open challenges for future research. First, accurately capturing highly dynamic details necessitates balancing temporal and spatial fidelity against limited context capacity. Second, long-form videos demand sophisticated strategies to navigate the trade-off between overall caption length and descriptive density while maintaining robust referential consistency for subjects over extended time horizons. Finally, stronger audiovisual integration is needed to accurately align acoustic and visual events and explicitly associate speakers with their utterances. The framework developed in this section focuses on absolute video descriptions, detailing the objective content of target video. Reference-conditioned generation, however, introduces new operational constraints: the caption should additionally specify reference bindings, isolate preserved attributes, and describe relative transformations while maintaining compatibility with the existing textual conditioning interface. The engineering principles governing this relative semantic contract are discussed in the next section.

sections.title: 4 Reference-Grounded Captioning: Orchestrating Coherent Multimodal Anchors
sections.content: Reference-conditioned generation enables controllable video creation through multimodal references, such as character portraits, source clips, and voice tracks. However, introducing reference conditions creates demanding correspondence problem. Each reference requires explicit binding to the correct target entity, property, modality, and temporal interval. Without precise alignment, generated video may appear perceptually flawless while suffering from critical systemic failures, such as exchanged identities, leaked attributes, edited protected content, or broken state continuity. Reference-grounded captioning (RGC) describes target videos conditioned on one or more multimodal references. Extending the semantic interface from Section 3, RGC explicitly specifies reference-target bindings, modified

At training scale, simply pairing references with conventional captions leaves these relationships implicit, causing the generator to learn global appearance correlations without reliable entity-level control. RGC resolves this problem by making the intended correspondences explicit, thereby providing robust supervision for both reference fidelity and controlled modification. sections.title: 4.1 Task Definition: Reference Semantics and Systemic Challenges
sections.content: Rather than generating an unconstrained summary from target video, reference assets, and task instructions, RGC defines the resulting caption as an integration of three distinct components: explicit pointers linking reference assets to target entities, supplementary descriptions capturing unreferenced facts, and scoped preservation or change records preventing text-reference conflicts. Crucially, RGC requires determining the scope of each references authority, which is asymmetric across properties. For instance, portrait may dictate facial identity while leaving body pose free; source video may lock background geometry while licensing requested localized edit; and an audio clip may define voice or rhythm without dictating visual action. sections.content: Reference-target confusion: Populating scene with multiple entities introduces severe combinatorial assignment ambiguity, especially when the references are semantically similar. Asymmetric modality authority: Different modalities naturally govern distinct properties (e.g., pixels for appearance, audio for timbre, video for motion), yet explicit instructions can selectively override these priors, requiring dynamic conflict resolution at the granular level of entities, attributes, and temporal intervals. Temporal binding persistence: Maintaining consistent identity associations across time is inherently fragile. Degenerate shortcuts: Models can artificially inflate precision by omitting entity IDs, using vague phrasing, or skipping complex edits entirely. Although factually safe, these shortcuts starve the generator of essential supervision, necessitating strict evaluation of required coverage alongside correctness.

RGC lets us turn any two videos with sufficient visual or acoustic similarity into training data for the DiT.

sections.content: The similarity may cover only part of the content. Two videos can show similar action performed by different people in different surroundings. The caption uses the reference for the shared movement and writes out the targets appearance, setting, and differences in the performance. Two recordings of the same speaker can likewise share voice while differing in words and delivery. The target dialogue and its timing remain in the caption. In either case, the annotation specifies which part of the target the reference supplies, in accordance with the scope established above. This expands the supply of training data beyond purpose-built editing pairs. target clip can be paired with several references: it may share subject with one clip and motion pattern with another. Each pairing asks the DiT to use its reference differently. The target remains fixed, but the caption and the content drawn from the reference both change. One video can therefore contribute several reference-conditioned examples alongside its standard caption. The number and variety of useful training pairs can grow with the video collection, without producing separate edited result for every pair. Training on this wider range of pairs strengthens the Omni DiTs ability to follow visual and acoustic conditions. Each example requires it to use the relevant content from the reference and produce the differences described by the caption, including changes that unfold over time. This improvement is reflected in reference fidelity and in edits that change the intended content while preserving the rest. The captions retain the target coverage and conventions of standard captioning, allowing standard and reference-conditioned data to be used together.

sections.content: Any sufficiently similar video pair is potential training example for the DiT. Relational annotation makes the pair usable by stating what to retain and what to change.

sections.title: 4.7 Discussion
sections.content: Future work could increase the flexibility of reference content and composition. Key directions include supporting diverse input forms (e.g., selected regions, sketches, and trajectories), enabling complex multimodal combinations to jointly specify single target, and developing finer-grained temporal binding for precise synchronization and transitions. Advancing these areas requires targeted supervision and evaluation. In real-world inference, user requests typically offer references and brief instructions without specifying the complete binding structure or scope of each reference. The remaining challenge is therefore to translate these underspecified requests into the same scoped, residual-sufficient, and authority-consistent caption distribution used during training. We address this challenge through PE in the following section.

sections.title: 5 Prompt Enhancement: From User Intent to the Caption Distribution
sections.content: Captioning determines the language that the generator learns (Sections 3 and 4); PE determines whether inference-time requests arrive in that language. Production requests are often short and colloquial or, increasingly, long passages written by other AI models, whereas the generator is trained on dense captions that describe subjects, action phases, camera movements, lighting, shots, and sound with consistent vocabulary and sentence style. PE rewrites request into condition drawn from this caption distribution while preserving the users intent [72]. HunyuanVideo established learned prompt rewriting for video generation [19], and RAPO showed that retrieval can move prompts toward the training distribution [9]. We split PE into two modules (Figure 5). Basic PE is the trained rewriter that produces the final condition in the caption dialect. Agentic PE runs before it at inference and decides what that condition should contain: it makes the story coherent and retrieves compelling examples. Our experience across Kling releases can be distilled into five lessons, the first three concerning basic PE and the last two concerning agentic PE. (1) PE output must match captions in wording and sentence patterns as well as in format; we achieve this by constructing data backward from captions of compelling videos. (2) Much of the gain comes from making the text faithful, reasonable, and vivid, which can be verified and optimized without running the generator. (3) Reinforcement learning (RL) with the DiT in the loop then aligns PE with product objectives and stabilizes quality, at measurable cost in peak vividness. (4) Contradictions in AI-written prompts are best resolved by story-refinement step before basic PE. (5) Retrieving compelling captions raises vividness, provided that training uses strict rejection sampling.

sections.title: 5.1 Basic PE: Caption Alignment through Backward Construction
sections.content: A user request always contains text and may also include images, videos, or audio clips as references. Basic PE rewrites only the text. It keeps every reference pointer in the instruction intact but does not modify the attached media, which reach the generator unchanged (Section 4). The alignment problem discussed below therefore concerns the text condition alone. Two conditions with similar semantics can produce visibly different videos when their length, slot order, terminology, or sentence structure differ. generic LLM rewriter tends to write metaphors, evaluative adjectives, motivational clauses, and long subordinate sentences. Such text reads well but lies outside the caption distribution: the generator spends conditioning capacity on language patterns it has rarely seen and may ignore controls phrased in unfamiliar terms. We therefore require alignment at three levels: format, meaning field order, length regime, and shot and timestamp markers; lexicon, meaning the camera, lighting, and action terms of the caption pipeline; and sentence patterns, meaning the declarative, present-tense, entity-explicit sentences of production captions. Matching format alone leaves the other two levels free to drift. Figure 6 contrasts typical generic rewrites with caption-aligned output at each level. sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: The most reliable way to achieve alignment at all three levels is to use real captions as training targets. We construct the data backward: starting from the caption of real video, teacher model writes the user prompt that could have produced it, and PE learns the mapping from prompt to caption. Synthetic prompts follow the statistics of real traffic rather than the teachers own style. For each pair we sample target length, language mixture, register, typo rate, and set of omitted slots from logged queries, and include references, multi-shot requests, and explicit exclusions at their observed frequencies. Prompts that leak the captions skeleton, for example by listing every action phase in caption order, are rejected, since PE would otherwise learn copying instead of completion. Exclusions follow the same principle. Captions describe what is visible, so PE rewrites no people as an empty street with unobstructed pavement and routes exclusions without positive equivalent either to negative-conditioning field or to sampling-time rejection. Backward construction also fixes the creative ceiling of PE, because the model learns to write like its target captions. If source captions are random sample of training videos, most targets describe ordinary footage with static framing and uneventful action, and PE learns to expand every request into competent but flat description. We therefore draw source captions mainly from videos that are compelling in themselves, such as professionally shot scenes, performances with clear dramatic beats, and clips with deliberate camera design, selected using aesthetic and motion scores and the vividness metric of Section 5.2. Domain and length quotas prevent this selection from collapsing onto few genres.

sections.title: Observation
sections.content: PE inherits the temperament of its target captions. When source captions are drawn uniformly from the training corpus, PE outputs are well formed and faithful but dull: different requests converge to similar generic framing, even lighting, and uneventful action. Choosing compelling source videos addresses this in the data, before any change to the model or the objective.

sections.title: 5.2 Text-Level Quality: Faithfulness, Reasonableness, and Vividness
sections.content: Optimizing PE through the generator is expensive: every rollout requires video sampling and judging, and video-level rewards are noisy. large fraction of the end-to-end gain is available earlier, from the text alone. Reasonableness deserves particular attention. The DiT is trained almost exclusively on real or carefully produced videos, so it has rarely seen condition that describes an impossible scene. When the text contains spatial contradiction, an object that changes identity, or an interaction without physical cause, the generator has no supervised behavior to fall back on and improvises freely. The result appears as identity drift, inconsistent layouts, objects passing through one another, or hands that never make contact. Unreasonable text is thus one of the most direct causes of consistency and interaction failures. We measure three properties, each scored on scale from 1 to 5, and use them in two places: every supervised fine-tuning (SFT) pair must pass all three verifiers, and the same scores serve as rewards for text-level RL. Faithfulness measures whether the output preserves user intent. judge decomposes the user prompt into checklist of atomic requirements covering entities, attributes, counts, actions, spatial relations, camera instructions, quoted text, audio, reference bindings, and exclusions. It then marks each item in the PE output as satisfied, violated, or unaddressed. Violations weigh more than omissions, and an addition that contradicts an item counts as violation. The checklist makes the score attributable, because regression can be traced to the requirement type that failed. Reasonableness measures whether the described video could exist. The judge reads the output sentence by sentence and incrementally builds two graphs. The spatial graph links entities by relative position, contact, containment, and viewpoint over time; the interaction graph links agents, actions, and patients together with their preconditions and resulting states. Each new sentence is checked against both graphs and against world knowledge: whether positions remain consistent, whether an object used in an action is present, whether result follows from its cause, and whether the number of events fits the duration. Each conflict lowers the score and is reported together with the sentence that introduced it. For example, in the man sets the cup on the table and walks to the door; he takes sip as he opens it, the spatial graph places the cup on the table and the man at the door, so the final interaction lacks its object. generator conditioned on this text must either duplicate the cup or teleport it, and both outcomes appear as artifacts.

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: Vividness measures expressive richness. The judge extracts expressive elements along several axes, including performance and facial expression, camera movement and shot design, lighting and color, pacing, and sound design. It matches them against curated library of professional techniques compiled from compelling videos and cinematographic references, and the score increases with the number of distinct, contextually appropriate hits. Hits are deduplicated per axis and capped, and only elements that pass the reasonableness check are counted, so stacking technical terms does not raise the score. Text-level RL uses GRPO to optimize reward that combines the three scores [43]. Faithfulness should gate the other terms: an output that violates an explicit requirement earns no credit for vividness, which prevents the policy from trading intent for spectacle. distribution term can additionally penalize outputs that fall outside the caption length and vocabulary regime, protecting the alignment of Section 5.1. Because no video is rendered, this stage is cheap enough to cover many prompts and iterations, and it precedes any DiT-in-the-loop training.

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: Solve text problems in text. Faithfulness, reasonableness, and vividness can be verified without rendering single frame. Removing these defects before involving the generator makes end-to-end RL cheaper and its rewards easier to interpret, because the remaining failures are more likely to be genuine generation limits.

sections.title: 5.3 DiT-in-the-Loop RL
sections.content: Text-level judges approximate what the generator needs, but they cannot observe how specific checkpoint responds to condition. In the final training stage, we connect PE to the frozen text encoder and DiT, sample several rewrites per prompt, render video for each, and update PE with group-relative policy gradient on video-level rewards. All three rewards come from the decision reward model of Section 7: visual quality and motion quality, the latter covering structural, physical, and temporal artifacts, are read from its taxonomy fields, and text alignment between the rendered video and the user prompt is scored by its checklist fields (Section 7.2). This stage aligns PE with product objectives and checkpoint-specific behavior, including which camera moves the current model executes reliably, while reducing quality variance across prompts and seeds. The order of the stages matters. DiT-in-the-loop RL starts from the text-level RL checkpoint, so its rollouts are already faithful, reasonable, and vivid, and the video rewards spend their limited sample budget on checkpoint-specific behavior instead of on defects that text judge could have caught. Because each update requires rendering several videos per prompt, this stage uses far fewer prompts than text-level RL, and those prompts are chosen to cover product domains and the failure slices found in production.

sections.title: Observation
sections.content: DiT-in-the-loop RL raises the floor and lowers the ceiling. After this stage, severe failures become rarer and worst-case quality improves. At the same time, the most impressive outputs become less impressive: PE learns to avoid complex choreography, large camera moves, and dense interactions, which are precisely the descriptions with the highest artifact risk. plausible explanation is that all three rewards penalize risk. None of them measures whether video is exciting, and conservative condition is the easiest way to avoid low score. Candidate remedies include keeping the vividness reward in the end-to-end objective, regularizing the policy toward the text-level RL checkpoint, and selecting checkpoints based on ceiling as well as floor metrics. Rewarding ambition directly without reintroducing artifacts remains an open problem.

sections.title: 5.4 Agentic PE: Story Refinement and Retrieval
sections.content: Basic PE is trained primarily for faithfulness. Reasonableness and vividness act on it as floors: its output must be no less reasonable and no less vivid than the users input, and every detail it adds must itself be reasonable. It is not, however, the place where the input itself is rethought: repairing contradiction that the user wrote would require departing from that input. Agentic PE takes that role at inference. It runs

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: before basic PE and performs two steps: story refinement makes the requested plot coherent, and retrieval supplies captions of compelling videos as creative evidence. Its output is still user-level specification plus optional context; basic PE always writes the final condition, so the caption dialect learned in Sections 5.15.3 is preserved regardless of what agentic PE adds. This division keeps creative decisions inspectable and lets each part be evaluated against its own objective. In production, many user prompts are themselves written by AI models through scripting Story Refinement assistants or upstream agent pipelines. These prompts are long and fluent but often internally inconsistent: characters clothing changes between paragraphs, scene is both indoors and outdoors, more events are planned than the duration allows, or an action depends on an object that was never introduced. Asking basic PE alone to repair them places two conflicting goals on one model, since faithfulness asks it to preserve what the user wrote while reasonableness asks it to change it. Story refinement resolves this conflict upstream. It works at the level of plot and leaves caption language to basic PE. It detects contradictions with the same spatial and interaction graphs used for reasonableness scoring, applies minimal edits that restore coherence while keeping the core intent, and passes the revised prompt on. Basic PE treats the refined prompt as authoritative and concentrates on translation into the caption distribution, without pressure to silently rewrite the story. Story refinement follows three rules. First, explicit hard constraints such as quoted dialogue, counts, reference bindings, and requested camera moves are never edited unless two of them conflict, in which case the refiner makes the smallest change that resolves the conflict and records the decision. Second, its edits are minimal and local: the refiner reorders, merges, or drops events and fixes attributes, but does not introduce new characters or change the premise. Third, its output is checked by the reasonableness judge and by faithfulness checklist computed on the non-conflicting part of the original prompt, before it reaches basic PE. When no coherent edit exists, the refiner can pass the prompt through unchanged with conflict flag, so that the product can ask the user instead of guessing. Retrieval of Compelling Captions Retrieval raises vividness further by showing basic PE how compelling videos with similar content are actually described [9]. The index contains captions from the same pool of compelling videos used for backward construction. For each refined request, agentic PE retrieves the top five captions and passes them as context. Basic PE decides which camera patterns, performance details, lighting setups, or sound designs suit the request. Letting the model choose among several candidates avoids dependence on single top hit, which often matches the topic but not the intended action or tone. Training basic PE to use this context requires strict rejection sampling. Retrieved captions contain specific entities, scene layouts, brands, and dialogue. If training targets copy such details, the model learns to import content the user never requested, form of hallucination that the faithfulness checklist detects only partially. For each training prompt we sample multiple candidates with retrieval context and reject any candidate that introduces an entity, attribute, or event that cannot be traced to either the user prompt or deliberate and compatible borrowing from retrieved caption. Surviving candidates must also pass all three text verifiers. The training set further includes cases in which all five retrieved captions are irrelevant and the accepted target ignores them, so that the model treats retrieval as optional evidence.

sections.title: 5.6 Discussion
sections.content: PE translates user intent into the language the generator was trained on, and it does so through two modules. Basic PE owns the caption dialect. Backward construction from compelling videos aligns its output with captions in format, wording, and sentence patterns, while also setting its creative ceiling. Faithfulness, reasonableness, and vividness verification, applied first as data filter and then as text-level rewards, removes the defects most likely to make the generator improvise. DiT-in-the-loop RL aligns basic PE with product objectives and raises the quality floor, at current cost in peak vividness. Agentic PE owns the content: story refinement resolves contradictions in AI-written prompts, and retrieval supplies compelling examples, so that no single module carries every responsibility. Two directions remain open: rewards that credit ambitious but executable content, and joint training of agentic PE and basic PE against shared verifiers. Several extensions of agentic PE are ongoing work. In experimental versions it calls tools to edit the users image, video, or audio references, or to supply information that the request leaves out. We are also exploring low-resolution previews that expose composition and motion before full-resolution generation, 3D previsualization that fixes layout and camera paths in advance, and post-generation verification that checks the output against the request and triggers revision when it fails. The main bottlenecks are latency and cost, since every tool call, preview, or verification pass adds inference time and compute to request. We expect these costs to fall as inference efficiency improves.

sections.title: 6 Text Encoder: Perceptual Grounding for Conditioning
sections.content: Captioning, RGC, and PE establish the explicit semantic contract of our pipeline, translating visual evidence and user intent into dense, structured text (Sections 35). Yet critical last-mile question remains: does the model that reads this text actually understand what it describes? The text encoder (TE) plays this pivotal role by converting the text prompt into the continuous conditioning representations consumed by the DiT. At the level of the generator, this conditioning interface can be written abstractly as Hcond = Φθ(c), (cid:98)v = Gϕ(Hcond, ϵ) , (1) where denotes the text prompt, Φθ the TE, Gϕ the video generator, and ϵ the sampling randomness. Because Gϕ observes the prompt solely through the sequence representation Hcond, any visual or temporal semantics left unresolved by Φθ cannot reach the generator, no matter how faithfully is written upstream. To make Hcond reliable conditioning signal for video generation, the TE must internalize visual, spatial, and temporal knowledge and express semantics across multiple granularitiesspanning fine-grained lexical details, mid-level relational layouts, and global narrative structure. Large text encoders offer substantial representational potential: their parameter counts provide ample capacity, while extensive pre-training

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: exposes them to broad lexical, relational, and conceptual structures. However, this potential does not automatically translate into effective video conditioning. Existing approaches typically rely directly on off-the-shelf TE weights and expose the DiT to features from only single encoder layer, even when inserting small-parameter auxiliary modules such as lightweight connectors or token refiners between the TE and the DiT [19]. Using unadapted backbone weights while collapsing the encoder output to single layer leaves much of its representational capacity unused and discards distinctions needed for video generation. We therefore unlock this representational potential at both the backbone and interface levels by adapting the encoder for perceptual grounding and extracting multi-granular, training-stable conditioning sequence. Across Kling iterations, our experience can be distilled into four core lessons: Sequence-level evaluation rather than general proxies. General QA benchmarks and single-vector retrieval fail to reflect how DiT consumes full sequence representations. Perceptual adaptation rather than reliance on off-the-shelf backbones. Current foundation models prioritize agentic skills over perception, and even MLLMs are trained on broad task mixtures. These trends motivate adaptation for spatiotemporal grounding. Multi-granular semantic conditioning. Video generation requires preserving literal details, relations, temporal structure, and global narrative context in one usable condition. The multi-layer representations of the TE provide complementary levels of abstraction that support these granularities. stable conditioning interface. The multi-layer conditioning representation must remain stable as the diffusion generator progresses across noise regimes and training stages.

sections.title: 6.1 Representation Evaluation Beyond General Proxies
sections.content: Selecting TE requires measuring whether its frozen hidden states resolve prompt as fine-grained scene specification. However, common lightweight proxiesgeneral comprehension benchmarks and retrieval metricsare structurally mismatched with how DiT uses the encoder [22]. When serving as TE, the encoder performs only prefill forward pass and supplies sequence of token-level hidden states Hcond to the DiT. General QA and comprehension benchmarks instead evaluate autoregressive decoding, measuring generated token outputs rather than the underlying hidden states used for conditioning. Cross-modal retrieval, meanwhile, evaluates single-vector matching, pooling the entire prompt into one vector rather than preserving the sequence dimension that the DiT attends to throughout generation. Evaluating TE for video conditioning should therefore operate directly on sequence-level hidden states [22].

sections.title: Observation
sections.content: General evaluation proxies are structurally mismatched with DiT conditioning. DiT conditions on the full sequence of prefill hidden states, whereas QA benchmarks evaluate autoregressively decoded outputs and retrieval metrics evaluate pooled single-vector representations; neither proxy directly measures the representation interface consumed by the generator. Effective TE screening should therefore probe the sequence of prefill hidden states on minimally contrasting descriptions [22]. Such fine-grained semantic contrasts enable rapid text-only filtering of candidate backbones and post-training checkpoints before costly end-to-end DiT training.

sections.title: 6.2 Adapting Foundation Backbones for Video Conditioning
sections.content: Current foundation models increasingly prioritize agentic capabilities over multimodal perception. Even among multimodal models, training spans wide variety of task types with heavy emphasis on visually grounded agent workflows. While such broad supervision produces versatile general-purpose assistants, it does not specialize the backbones hidden states for the dense spatiotemporal grounding required by video conditioning. Empirical evidence supports this distinction: although multimodal pre-training improves generative conditioning over pure-text LLMs, broad multi-task instruction tuning offers no reliable gain, and reasoning-oriented post-training can even degrade prefill hidden states when it shifts capacity from descriptive grounding toward step-by-step deduction [22]. We therefore strengthen the TE through targeted multimodal adaptation rather than relying on off-the-shelf

sections.title: Multimodal Understanding behind Kling Video Generation
sections.content: weights. We build on Kling-MLLM (Section 2), which already provides stronger spatiotemporal perception than general Qwen backbones, and further adapt it using dense video descriptions and perceptual understanding tasks (Section 3). This adaptation enhances the perceptual representation capacity of Φθ in Eq. 1, allowing its hidden states to more faithfully encode the visual and temporal details specified in the prompt.

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: Perceptual adaptation strengthens the TE for video conditioning. Training the backbone on dense descriptions and spatiotemporal perception tasks enhances its ability to resolve visual and temporal details in its hidden states, providing stronger conditioning representations.

sections.title: 6.3 Multi-Granular Semantic Conditioning
sections.content: Beyond adapting the backbone weights, effective conditioning also depends on how features are extracted from the TE. Video-generation prompts are inherently multi-granular and hierarchical: at the local level, they specify visible text, appearance, and instantaneous actions; at the relational level, they bind attributes to entities and encode spatial or temporal interactions; at the global level, they organize scene context, shot progression, and narrative intent. The TE exhibits related hierarchy across its depth, with different layers capturing complementary levels of lexical, relational, and conceptual abstraction [12, 23]. Exposing only single layer to the DiT therefore creates structural mismatch between the multi-granular prompt and the representation supplied to the generator. Instead, the conditioning interface should aggregate information across encoder layers so that local details remain anchored to relational structure and global scene context.

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: A multi-granular prompt requires multi-layer condition. Aggregating complementary encoder layers preserves lexical details, entity relations, temporal structure, and global context in one sequence representation rather than forcing single layer to carry every level of abstraction.

sections.title: 6.4 Stable Conditioning During Diffusion Training
sections.content: Combining features across multiple TE layers typically relies on learnable fusion module optimized alongside the DiT. However, diffusion training is inherently non-stationary: the generator primarily optimizes coarsegrained structure in early training and gradually shifts toward fine-grained details in later stages, while training configurations such as timestep sampling and video resolution also change across stages. Because different TE layers capture different semantic granularities, these shifting optimization targets continuously pull the fusion module toward different layer combinations. Rather than converging to stationary weighting, the fusion module exhibits fusion instabilityits layer weights continue to drift or fluctuate throughout training [22, 23]. Even when the TE backbone itself is frozen, an unstable fusion module makes the fused representation Hcond non-stationary. As the fusion weights drift across training stages, the conditioning distribution supplied to the DiT shifts accordingly, forcing the generator to repeatedly re-adapt to the same text prompt. Stabilizing the fusion module is therefore essential to prevent conditioning drift and maintain consistent semantic interface across all stages of diffusion training [22, 23].

sections.title: Insight
sections.content: Unstable multi-layer fusion creates non-stationary condition. As diffusion training shifts from coarse structure to fine-grained details across stages, learnable fusion weights tend to drift; stabilizing the fusion module keeps the condition from becoming moving target for the DiT.

sections.title: 6.6 Discussion
sections.content: The TE is more than passive linguistic lookup module attached to the DiT: it is the component that maps multimodal understanding into the continuous conditioning space of the generator. While captioning, RGC, and PE express multimodal understanding explicitly as structured text, the TE converts that text into an implicit, multi-granular scene representationscreened at the sequence level, adapted for spatiotemporal perception, aggregated across encoder layers, and stabilized throughout diffusion training.

sections.title: 7 Reward Models: Turning Understanding into an Optimization Signal
sections.content: The preceding sections construct semantic contract across the video generation pipeline: captioning specifies what training videos contain, RGC states what should be preserved or modified, PE translates user requests into that contract, and the TE determines which distinctions reach the generator. Post-training and inferencetime selection require an explicit optimization direction to enforce this contract: among candidate rollouts, the system must determine which video should be assigned higher probability and identify which specific regions or time intervals failed and why. reward model (RM) supplies this executable utility signal.

sections.title: 7.1 Objectives, Challenges, and Application Scenarios
sections.content: Building MLLM-based video RMs across successive Kling generations exposed three challenges: 1. Perceptual bandwidth before reasoning depth. For generated-video defects, visual perception is tighter bottleneck than language reasoning [26]. Scaling general-purpose MLLM or eliciting long chain of thought (CoT) does not improve artifact detection if the vision tower is insensitive to low-level synthesis distortions, or if transient anatomical and physical anomalies are erased by sparse frame sampling and token compression [49]. 2. Dimensional entanglement and loser-centric attribution bias. Video quality decomposes into at least four axesvisual quality (VQ), motion quality (MQ), consistency, and text alignment (TA)each with finer sub-dimensions  (Table 16)  [28]. In human pairwise annotations, however, dimensions are strongly coupled with overall preference, and defect attributions are loser-centric: annotators reliably record the decisive flaw of the losing video but frequently leave the winning videos defects unannotated. Treating unannotated winners as clean negatives or deriving criteria from candidate contrasts with metadata shortcuts [31], corrupts the decision boundary.

sections.title: 7.2 Model Design
sections.content: Built on Kling-MLLM-27B (Section 2), our pipeline unifies all supervision sources under hierarchical evaluation taxonomy  (Table 16)  spanning four Level-1 categories, ten Level-2 dimensions, and fine-grained leaf defect tags. Each L2 dimension is scored on its own rather than only through an overall preference, so that reward can be traced to the dimension that produced it and dimension can be added when optimization exposes blind spot. Training progresses through three stages (Figure 7). Observation Penalizing artifacts alone rewards stillness. generator optimized against defect penalties can lower its risk by moving less, and slow or frozen video contains few anatomical or physical errors. Motion magnitude is therefore scored as dimension of its own and acts as counterweight in DiT RL. Stage 1: Visual Adaptation for Low-Level Artifact Perception. General-purpose vision encoders are pretrained for semantic recognition, which encourages invariance to high-frequency texture noise, frame-to-frame flicker, and local geometric distortions [26]. In Stage 1, we freeze the LLM and optimize only the vision encoder and aligner on two tasks: (1) VAE reconstruction discrimination, pairing natural clips with VAE-decoded counterparts to sensitize the encoder to subtle blur, codec, and smoothing artifacts; and (2) templated defect probes derived from RL-pair and single-video defect logs. Frame sampling is tailored to the dimension being judged: densely sampled frames are used for motion and artifact dimensions, whereas sparsely sampled frames at native high resolution are used for VQ dimensions. Retaining 20% Stage 1 replay in later stages prevents catastrophic forgetting of low-level visual discrimination. Observation judge cannot reason about defect it does not see. Longer chains of thought do not recover an artifact that the vision encoder smooths away or that sparse frame sampling skips, and many anatomical and physical anomalies last under two seconds. Perception has to be trained before judgment.

sections.content: Figure 7 Three-stage training pipeline for our RMs, starting from Kling-MLLM-27B. Stage 1 adapts the vision encoder and aligner with the LLM frozen for low-level artifact perception; Stage 2 trains the General Reward Model (GRM) with cold-start SFT and RL with verifiable rewards for explainable evaluation; Stage 3 initializes the Decision Reward Model (DRM) from the GRM and performs decision-head warm-up, unified pointwisepairwise SFT with TA grounding, and symmetry calibration with gated inference for fast multi-dimensional scoring. Stage 2: GRM for Explainable Evaluation with Localized Evidence. Stage 2 unfreezes the backbone and trains the GRM on three sources: the training splits of open-source datasets (their validation and test splits are never used); our human-annotated forensic corpus, which specifies defect category, temporal interval [tstart, tend], per-frame bounding boxes, and rationale; and rubric-derived checklist VQA instances written without access to preference labels [31]. The GRM is trained in two steps: Step 1: Cold-start SFT. We fine-tune the GRM to produce structured critiques, defect evidence tubes (each consisting of temporal interval with per-frame boxes), and ordinal ratings in fixed output format; the probability-weighted expectation of the rating serves as its scalar score. Training uses 1 : 10 vision-to-LLM learning-rate ratio and 20% Stage 1 replay so that the low-level perception acquired in Stage 1 is preserved. Step 2: RL with verifiable rewards. We optimize = 8 rollouts per video via GRPO [43] with verifiable reward that is gated by output-format validity and combines four checkable terms: ordinal rating calibration against human scores, defect-presence correctness, tag-set F1 against the annotated defect categories, and spatiotemporal mIoU of the predicted intervals and bounding boxes. Unmatched ground-truth defects are penalized, so the policy cannot raise its reward by reporting fewer defects.
