The DRM is trained in three steps: Step 1: Decision-Head Warm-up. With the backbone frozen, we train only the decision head on generic multiple-choice corpora (VQA, preference, and tool-use samples), then unfreeze the full model on video critiques with vote-aggregated soft labels and on temporal localization. Each field is supervised with soft cross-entropy over its options, plus ranked probability score (RPS) term for ordinal fields. Step 2: Unified PointwisePairwise SFT and TA Grounding. We fine-tune jointly on single-video defect and checklist items and on two-video packs that carry per-video and pairwise fields, so that defect sensitivity and pairwise discrimination are learned in the same prefill. Text alignment is strengthened with instructionfollowing pairs and with audiovisual checklists comprising several atomic questions per video. As an auxiliary task, randomly sampled subset of checklist items in each training sample is paired with temporal fields, one binary field per one-second bin, to mark when the prompted event occurs; this anchors alignment decisions to the frames that support them and improves the judgment of event timing and temporal order. Step 3: Symmetry Calibration and Gated Inference. Causal/linear attention and M-RoPE [54] induce position bias across video order [70], and the worse and better fields of one dimension can disagree; averaging over swapped orders and both polarities costs two to four passes per pair. We instead place both polarities in one prefill and regularize training with (i) symmetric KL between the worse field and the option-swapped better field of each dimension and (ii) cross-order BradleyTerry loss [3] between original and order-swapped packs. At inference, confidence gate invokes the swapped pass only on low-margin cases, matching multipass accuracy at near-single-pass latency; when invoked, the second pass uses complementary dense/sparse frame sampling to catch transient collapses within the context limit.

sections.title: 8 Automatic Evaluation: Measuring What Each Task Requires
sections.content: Automatic evaluation serves as the measurement layer for video generation. While training loss can indicate optimization failures, it cannot directly assess whether generated videos satisfy task-specific requirements, such as correct actions, consistent identity preservation, or audiovisual alignment. These properties must instead be evaluated on the generated outputs. Accordingly, the objective is not to design single universal video quality score, but to determine four fundamental aspects of evaluation: the target task, the failure modes that matter, the tools capable of detecting them, and the reliability of the resulting measurements. Table 19 summarizes the first three aspects for each major task; measurement reliability is discussed below.

sections.title: 8.1 Task Taxonomy: What Should Be Evaluated?
sections.content: The evaluation protocol should be defined by the underlying generation task. Different tasks have distinct success criteria and correspondingly different failure modes. More importantly, they differ in the ways in which models can achieve high evaluation scores without genuinely satisfying the intended objective. Captioning. Lexical-overlap metrics such as BLEU and CIDEr penalize valid paraphrases and are poorly suited to dense video descriptions. Recent benchmarks therefore shift from wording similarity to semantic coverage, decomposing video content into atomic keypoints and verifying whether each fact is correctly expressed. VidCapBench [5] exemplifies this paradigm with 643 videos and 10,644 QA pairs spanning aesthetics, content, motion, and physical laws, while distinguishing items suitable for automatic evaluation from those requiring human judgment. CapRiCorn-1K [6] extends this paradigm to long videos by also evaluating referential consistency, testing whether entities remain consistently identified across time and shots. For comparative captioning, factual coverage alone is insufficient: similarities and differences must be evaluated separately, as in ViDiC [60]. Caption evaluation should also demonstrate downstream validity. VidCapBench reports correlations of 0.890.92 between caption accuracy and downstream text-to-video generation quality, while CapRiCorn-1K shows that caption quality correlates strongly with long-video reasoning and video reconstruction performance. These results highlight key criterion for caption evaluation: metric should guide data or captioner design only if improvements in the metric translate into measurable downstream gains. Text-driven Generation. Text-to-video evaluation should distinguish instruction following, perceptual quality, and physical or commonsense plausibility. VBench [17] decomposes video quality into 16 dimensions rather than collapsing them into single score, while VBench-2.0 [69] further extends evaluation to human fidelity, controllability, creativity, physics, and commonsense. For compositional prompts, attributes, spatial relations, interactions, and motion are evaluated with specialized tools, as no single similarity metric reliably captures

sections.content: all these aspects [47]. Audio introduces additional dimensions that must be evaluated independently. T2AVCompass [4] and LongAV-Compass [30] jointly assess video and audio quality, textvideo and textaudio alignment, audiovisual synchronization, instruction following, and realism. Their results reveal substantial asymmetry across these dimensions: strong video quality does not necessarily imply realistic audio or consistent materialtimbre correspondence. This distinction is fundamental: instruction-following checklists measure whether the requested content is present, whereas realism criteria assess whether that content is perceptually and physically plausible. Reference and Keyframe Control. Reference-conditioned generation requires more than embedding similarity. Evaluation should account for entity identity, fine-grained details, role binding, and natural integration. MultiRef-Compass [67] further introduces an anti-paste coefficient, EFfinal = EFbasePpaste, which penalizes direct copying of reference content and prevents copypaste behavior from inflating fidelity scores. Keyframe-conditioned generation introduces an additional temporal dimension: detecting whether keyframe appears is necessary but insufficient. KeyFrame-Compass [48] therefore decomposes keyframe response into presence, visual fidelity, temporal order, temporal position, persistence, and response uniqueness. This decomposition distinguishes successful temporal integration from failure modes such as slideshow-like transitions, transient flashes, prolonged freezes, and reversed sequences. The same principle generalizes to other temporally controlled settings, including firstand last-frame-conditioned generation, shot planning, and camera trajectory control. (2) Editing. Video editing must satisfy two competing objectives: the requested content should change, while unrelated content should remain intact. CoVEBench [61] decomposes complex editing instructions into atomic checks and separately evaluates instruction compliance, output quality, and source fidelity. AVE-Compass [57] extends this evaluation to joint audiovideo editing. Its Editing Intent score is defined for each case and each modality as EI(c) = IF(c) FP(c) , (3) where IF measures instruction following and FP measures fidelity preservation. The multiplicative formulation ensures that neither leaving the source unchanged nor regenerating it indiscriminately can achieve high score. Response gating provides an additional safeguard: preservation and realism are evaluated only when the target modality responds to the edit, while non-responses are retained as instruction-following failures.

sections.title: 8.2 Evaluation Tools and Reliability: How Can Each Property Be Measured Accurately?
sections.content: No single tool observes every property of generated video. Signal-based and embedding-based metrics such as DOVER++, CLIP, CLAP, and Synchformer are inexpensive and stable, yet they capture only global quality and similarity. Specialist perception models, including detectors, trackers, and identity or speech models, add localized evidence about where and when an entity or change appears. MLLM checklist judges [14] cover the remaining semantic requirements that resist simple measurement. In practice, each property is routed to the simplest tool able to observe it reliably, with specialist evidence grounding the semantic judgments. Accurate evaluation, however, depends as much on protocol design as on the tools themselves. Holistic ratings should be replaced by atomic, directly observable criteria, and competing requirements should be scored jointly so that trivial shortcutssuch as leaving video unedited or pasting referencecannot inflate the result. Frame rate, resolution, and token budget belong to the protocol rather than to implementation details; genuine temporal metric must change when temporal evidence is removed or shuffled [36]. Automatic judges also require calibration against human annotations and explicit control of known biases [70], together with fixed configuration for reproducibility. Finally, reporting results per dimension and difficulty slice exposes weaknesses that single aggregate score would hide, while hidden prompts and periodic human review guard against benchmark overfitting.

sections.content: The same evaluation taxonomy can be instantiated at three cost levels. An hourly smoke test relies on deterministic signal-based metrics and small set of high-agreement checklist items. daily regression board

These levels differ in evaluator configuration and rigor rather than merely in the number of evaluated samples. Evaluation outputs should ultimately support diagnosis. For each failure, the system should retain the evaluation criterion, sampled evidence, tool outputs, judge rationale, and likely upstream source. Caption failures should be traced back to annotation or captioning, reference-binding failures to conditioning, realism failures to generation or reward modeling, and evaluator disagreements to protocol calibration. useful benchmark should therefore do more than rank models: it should identify which capability fails, under what conditions, and where in the generation pipeline the failure originates.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: This report summarizes the observations and insights into multimodal understanding that we gained from successive generations of Kling, viewing generation quality as the projection of understanding through the entire dataconditioningalignmentevaluation chain. Kling-MLLM, shared multimodal foundation model, provides the perceptual foundation for every downstream module. Captioning serves as dense semantic contract for training, and RGC extends this contract with explicit reference bindings. PE translates user intent into this caption distribution, with agentic steps that refine the story and retrieve compelling examples. reliable TE comes from perceptual training and multi-layer fusion, and candidate TEs can be screened from text alone. Reward modeling pairs an explainable GRM with fast DRM, treating perceptual bandwidth as primary design parameter. For automatic evaluation, our review suggests that protocols should follow the task, expose scoring shortcuts, and help trace failures to their upstream source. We hope these lessons offer practical guidance for building the understanding stack that supports controllable video generation.
